One term fails the test. "Pin" arrives unexplained in a sentence that makes a claim about what a pin does, and the reader has to infer its meaning from the earlier checksum sentence. The other gaps are minor: "reliance risk" and "retained results" depend on a link, while "the extractor" and "locator" are left for the reader to infer. Context mostly recovers these, so they are recorded as info.

# Review

The H1 says a citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved. The body supports a version of this claim. The section "Which evidence a pass is relative to" says the binding stops at the capture and that missing bytes report as unverified. So the title is not false to the body.

The title is narrower than the body, and it phrases the claim along a different axis. The body opens with what a citation asserts. It then spends most of its length on what a quote check can and cannot establish: wording only (not attribution, context or truth), relative to a normalization rule, unambiguous only under a uniqueness constraint, and relative to whichever evidence was used. The capture is one possible evidence base among several, and the body also discusses intermediary extracts and the absence of any evidence. A title that tracks the body would name quote checking, or the relativity of a pass to its compared evidence, rather than citation fidelity bounded by a capture.

# Review

## Summary

The note's strongest claim, using only its own commitments, is this: a quote check's pass certifies only that the span occurs, under a stated normalization rule, in the evidence the check actually used. Fidelity to the original, attribution, context and truth stay unverified unless separate checks establish them. The title compresses that claim well.

The body does not lead with it. The opening paragraph explains what an exact-quotation marker asserts and the one relation a quote check tests. Next come the four-question taxonomy, then normalization and occurrence. Only in "Which evidence a pass is relative to" does the note say plainly that a pass is relative to the compared evidence and that the binding stops at the capture. The description frames the note as a general survey of quote checking. That matches the body's order better than the title does, so the title's claim competes with sections that have the same weight.

The material itself is defensible and mostly serves the claim: normalization and occurrence are further ways a pass can say less than it seems to. Its order and framing hide that role. The simplest fix is to state in the opening that a pass is relative to the evidence used and that the capture-to-original link is unchecked. The existing sections can then read as elaborations of that limit.

A possible revision target, separate from this verdict: the note could unify all four sections under one claim, that a pass is relative to its rule, its occurrence constraint and its evidence. The current text implies this framing but does not state it.

# Review

The note is mostly compact. The four-question list, the normalization and occurrence paragraphs, the multi-read paragraph and the scope bullets each add a distinct condition or boundary. The closing sentence on verified source extracts turns the preceding mechanism into an operational recommendation, so it is not flagged as recap.

The section "Which evidence a pass is relative to" has two local redundancies. First, the pin sentences repeat when change gets detected before they add the one new limit. Second, the rule against falling back to another copy appears in the source-identity paragraph and again in the following paragraph. Each case calls for a fold, not a deletion: in both, one clause carries information the other lacks.

The cost argument for treating a mismatch as a failure overlaps with the preceding paragraph's cheap-and-binary point. It may still earn a separate paragraph because of the trade-off link, so it is recorded as INFO only.

# Friction check: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Central claim (one sentence):** A quote check verifies only that a span occurs, under a stated normalization rule, in the specific evidence it compared, so a pass says nothing about attribution upstream of that evidence, contextual support or truth.

## Filter
**Filter:** SURVIVES

The claim commits to one consistent thing. A pass is relative to identified evidence, and the note keeps wording, attribution, context and truth separate without needing them to hold at once. The trade-off it handles, too little against too much normalization, is stated as a trade-off rather than wished away. The one strain is between the title and the body: the title speaks of what a citation can *assert* and limits it to a *capture*, while the body concerns what a check can *verify* against any evidence. That gap does not make the claim incompatible with itself, but it is the first joint listed below.

## Thinnest joints

The failure-semantics joint ranks thinnest because the note's own later paragraph says what it leaves out. Cost is given as the reason a mismatch can be a failure, while the normalization section shows that the reason is actually calibration against false mismatches. The title-to-body mismatch comes next. It is a document-level joint because no single sentence derives the title. The casebook evidence and the model-context exclusion are both locally plausible, but the reader has to supply the step each one relies on: that the hidden edits are substantive, and that unbound text cannot be identified. The support-blocking joint is the strongest of these five. It holds if "noisier" carries the argument, but it is phrased as an impossibility. The remaining joints hold under the skeptical default and are not listed: uniqueness removing ambiguity, forbidding concatenation, the limits of the identity binding, missing bytes reporting as unverified, excerpts losing context, and exact checks verifying only their own pair.

## For the human
Look first at the second paragraph under "Four questions, one answered mechanically": should cheapness or a calibrated normalization rule justify treating mismatch as failure? Then decide whether the title should say "verify" rather than "assert", and "evidence" rather than "capture".

# Critique: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Note:** kb/theory/a-citation-cannot-assert-more-fidelity-than-its-capture-preserved.md
**Central commitment:** A quote check establishes only that the quoted words occur, under a stated normalization rule, in the specific evidence it compared, so a passing citation is no more faithful to the original than the capture it was checked against.
**Critique mode:** claim
**Attack outcome:** partially lands

## Strongest case against it

Two objections reinforce each other.

First, the title is false as worded, and the note's first paragraph shows why. A citation is a speech act by its author. It asserts whatever its author claims: exact wording, attribution and implied faithful context. The note says this directly: "Unchecked, that assertion rests on the author's word." So citations routinely *assert* more fidelity than any capture preserved. What the body defends is a different claim: a *check* can *establish* fidelity only relative to the evidence it used ("A pass means 'agrees with the evidence this check used'"). The title confuses what is asserted with what can be verified. A reader who retrieves the note by its title gets a claim that the first paragraph contradicts.

Second, even the corrected claim ("a verified citation cannot establish more fidelity than its capture preserved") is a universal that a digital-provenance practitioner would reject. That practitioner might come from web archiving (Memento, multiple independent archives), content-authenticity work (signed manifests in the C2PA style, PGP-signed releases) or scholarly versioning (DOIs and versioned preprints with publisher hashes). In their view, fidelity to the original and attribution to an author are not bounded by one capture. Three mechanisms carry evidence past it:
- **Author or publisher signatures.** A signature over the bytes binds them to a key holder, so a check against a signed capture establishes attribution, the question the note says no mechanism answers.
- **Independent corroboration.** Two or more captures taken independently, by different parties at different times, that agree on the passage give evidence about the original that exceeds any one of them.
- **Content-addressed or immutable originals.** When the original itself is identified by hash, a capture that matches the hash *is* the original's bytes, so the capture-to-original gap closes.

On this view the note has presented a feature of its own mechanism, a checksum pin of one local capture, as a law about citations.

## How the note engages it

**Partially engaged.** On the second objection, the body is careful where the title is not. It limits the gap to "no mechanism *here*", lists attribution as a separate question that an identity check answers only "in part", and scopes transfer beyond agent-operated KBs as resting on reasoning alone. These hedges make the body consistent with the provenance practitioner's position: the body never claims that signatures or corroboration cannot close the gap; it simply does not use them. The title and the universal framing ("cannot") remove that hedge. The note names none of the three mechanisms, so a reader cannot tell whether the claim is "this system's checks stop at the capture" (true and well argued) or "no check can exceed its capture" (false for signed or content-addressed sources).

On the first objection, the note does not engage at all. Paragraph 1 distinguishes asserting from making the assertion falsifiable, which is exactly the distinction the title collapses.

The core mechanism survives: the separation of four questions, the "pass is relative to its evidence" principle, unverified-not-passed for missing bytes, and the location-versus-occurrence argument. The attack lands on the title's scope and wording, not on the body's reasoning.

## Constructive findings

- Retitle so the claim is about what a check establishes, for example "A quote check verifies fidelity only to the evidence it compared". The current title is contradicted by the note's own opening.
- In "Which evidence a pass is relative to", name the mechanisms that can carry evidence past one capture: author or publisher signatures, content-addressed originals and agreement among independent captures. Then say either that they are out of scope or that they move the evidential bound rather than abolish it. That turns the local "here" into an explicit, inspectable boundary.
- Qualify the closing sentence about verified source extracts: extracts avoid paraphrase compounding but can inherit the selection loss described two paragraphs earlier.

## Secondary objections (optional)

- "Wording agreement is deterministic, cheap and binary" holds only once a normalization rule is fixed. The next section shows that choosing the rule involves judgments about meaning (case, emphasis, typography). The sentence could say "binary given a fixed normalization rule", so it does not suggest that the wording question is free of judgment.
- The description emphasizes quote checking in general, while the title emphasizes the capture limit. The four-question decomposition, arguably the note's most reusable contribution, does not appear in the title. Retrieval by the decomposition may miss the note.

# Premise decomposition: A citation cannot assert more fidelity than its capture preserved

**Register:** claim
**Central commitment (one sentence):** A quote check can certify only that a quoted span occurs, under a stated normalization rule, in the identity-bound evidence the check actually used (usually a capture), so a passing citation establishes wording fidelity no further upstream than that evidence and leaves upstream attribution, contextual support and truth unverified.

## Premises and counterexamples

The commitment consumes three groups of premises:

- **What the check tests.** The four citation questions are separable, a string check answers only wording, and wording agreement is mechanical.
- **What "exact" and "pass" mean.** The normalization rule must be specified. Uniqueness or range removes ambiguity about the occurrence. A pass is relative to the evidence the check used.
- **What the evidence is bound to.** A checksum with explicit pairing binds the bytes to a capture and no further. Missing bytes are unverified. Rechecks catch passage change but not context change. Exact chains verify only their own pairs.

Most premises survived an active hunt, mainly because the note already concedes the cases a hunter would reach first: extractor gaps, untested locators, and context loss when a source is read in chunks.

Three premises are dented. None propagates to the commitment.

- **The upper bound.** The strongest dent is to the claim that attribution cannot be verified past the capture. The body scopes this with "here", but the description generalises it. Signed or content-addressed sources are a checkable counterexample to the general reading. They support the title and contradict the description, because a signature is something a capture can preserve.
- **Exact chains.** The claim that exact chains do not compose overlooks that occurrence is transitive. The note's real point is about non-contiguous extracts and mismatched rules.
- **What a pass is relative to.** The "relative to evidence" section drops the normalization rule from what a pass depends on, although the opening paragraph includes it.

All three repairs narrow or complete a premise. None weakens the commitment.

## For the human

Look first at the attribution premise ("The binding stops at the capture…"). The description promises that "attribution upstream" stays unverified in general, but a signed source's capture can carry attribution. Scope the claim to unsigned captures or to this check's mechanisms.

- Location: opening paragraph ("A quote check makes it falsifiable by testing one relation") through the first sentences of "Which evidence a pass is relative to" ("A pass means \"agrees with the evidence this check used\"", "The binding stops at the capture").

The four questions and the material on normalization and occurrence come before that limit. With equal weight, they read as a general survey of quote checking, which matches the description's framing rather than the title's.
- Direction: state in the opening that a pass certifies agreement only with the compared evidence and that nothing checks the capture against the original. Then let each section show one way a pass says less than it seems to. One possible resolution, not settled: a pass is relative to its normalization rule, its occurrence constraint and its evidence. The note implies that three-way framing but never states it. The core-claim check proposed it as a possible revision target.

- Preserve or decide: the title and the description choose different contributions. The title makes one claim about where fidelity stops; the description promises a survey of what each check establishes and what stays unverified. The body supports either reading. The author must choose. Retitling toward the survey keeps the current order. Keeping the title's claim requires the reordering above. If the three-way framing is adopted, keep the four-question taxonomy's distinct job: naming what stays unverified (context, truth, upstream attribution). It is not a fourth dimension of relativity.

### 2. Reduce the context and paraphrase branches to their bounding points

- Location: under "Which evidence a pass is relative to", the multi-read paragraph ("A model may need several reads…") and the closing sentences of the provenance paragraph ("Semantic hops compound instead…" through "…a paraphrase of a paraphrase.").

Cut the procedural rule (retrieve context and keep the full source outside the model's context) and the extract recommendation, or move them elsewhere. Moving the context point must not merge it with the wording check: the note's claim that context needs a reader of both texts must stay intact.

### 3. Present the evidence section's limits once, in order

- Location: section "Which evidence a pass is relative to", from the source-identity paragraph through the "Retained, accessible and used material differ" paragraph.
- Reader problem: the section that carries the title's claim repeats itself twice. One repeat covers the no-fallback rule: "not an invitation to find another copy" and the later "silent fallback… (ADR 073)". The other covers when change is detected: the pin sentence and the sentence on checking current bytes. The section's sequence of separate limits is therefore harder to follow than its content warrants.

Next, refusal to substitute another copy, stated once with its reason that ambient cache state would otherwise decide the result. Missing bytes report as unverified. The binding stops at the capture. Finally, a later check detects drift but misses changed surrounding context. The marginal-value check offered a folded pin sentence that illustrates one possible resolution.

- Preserve or decide: keep each distinct limit, as the detail-overhang check found that each sentence in the identity paragraph sets its own boundary. Specifically keep the blind spot for surviving quoted words in a changed context. Keep the rule that missing bytes are unverified, never passed. Keep the distinction between retained, accessible and used material. Keep the ADR 073 grounding attached to the no-fallback reason.
